The Rice Fund was introduced in 2021 by the Mayor's Task Force in collaboration with community members as a response to historic inequities and government funding.

It supports community groups and non-for-profit organizations led by and serving Black, Indigenous, and other racialized community members, advancing initiatives that promote equity, opportunity, and well-being across Kitchener.

Launched in 2022 as a three-year pilot with an initial $50,000 budget, the pilot was designed to collect evidence-based data, measure community impact, identify barriers, and assess the need for an increased investment.
Since then, applications have surged by 253%, growing with 41 applications in 2022 to 145 in 2024.
Over three years, 268 applications were received, totaling over $2 million in funding requests,
with projects and events as the most set out categories.
In response to evolving community needs, Council increased the RISE Fund Budget to $96,789
in 2022, followed by a commitment of $150,000 annually for 2023 and 2024.
This funding level will be sustained through 2025 and 2026, with a proposal for a long-term
sustainable funding model slated for 2027.
RISE is Kitchener's only fund dedicated to racialized communities.
Regionally, the Upstring Fund committed $2.89 million in 2024 and $1.9 million in 2025 to support equity initiatives,
while Waterloo Region Community Foundation's Racial Equity Fund invested $437,000 in 2024 and $300,000 in 2025.
RISE provides funding across four categories, capacity building, operational costs, projects,
and events.
Applicants may receive up to $10,000 annually for capacity building, operations, and project-based
initiatives and up to $5,000 per funding cycle for events.
In its first three years, the Rice Fund has delivered strong outcomes and meaningful community
impact.
A total of $3,000, $96,789 have been invested directly in Black, Indigenous, and other racialized
communities.
This investment has supported 54 initiatives led and delivered by 43 local groups and organizations.
Together these efforts have impacted more than 6,000 Kitchener residents.

The RISE Fund has made undeniable progress in advancing equity and community impact.
To build on this progress, staff have identified five key recommendations designed to enhance
access and opportunity, align funding priorities with the evolving needs of the community,
achieve a balanced approach that maximizes impact while ensuring operational and financial
sustainability and simplify logistics and program administration for applicants, the
selection committee and staff.
These recommendations aim to strengthen the fund's effectiveness, responsiveness and
sustainability.
First, staff propose refining the eligibility criteria.
The current broad approach has led to uneven competition between well-established organizations
and emerging groups.
To level the playing field, staff recommend prioritizing emerging groups operating for
five years or less, enhancing access to those with limited alternative funding options.
Indigenous communities will continue to be prioritized regardless of their operational
status.
Second, staff recommend streamlining the funding categories.
Nearly half of the past applications have focused on projects and events.
By narrowing the categories to these two with a $10,000 annual cap, we can better reflect
community priorities.
To maximize local impact, all funded projects and events must be held and delivered within
the City of Kitchener.
Third, staff propose simplifying the intake period.
The current two-cycle model has contributed to application fatigue and strained resources.
to an annual intake in the fall will encourage more strategic proposals, prioritize quality
over quantity, and create a more manageable workload for both the selection committee
and staff.
Fourth, we aim to strengthen capacity building.
Many applicants face barriers due to limited grant writing experience.
A comprehensive RISE fund guide paired with info sessions and workshops will support stronger
applications and long-term sustainability.
Finally, staff recommend re-evaluating the selection committee structure.
Currently, the Equity and Anti-Racism Advisory Committee serves in this role.
However, its mandate does not fully align with the fund's operational needs.
We will explore alternative models that offer more targeted expertise and capacity.
The first four recommendations, including updates to the application form and the evaluation rubric,
are scheduled to launch in 2026 and are expected to deliver immediate benefits.
Proposed changes to the committee structure will be brought forth in early 2027.
In conclusion, the Rice Fund was created in direct response to the voices of racialized residents
calling for meaningful and sustained support.
It also embodies Kitchener's commitment to reconciliation, equity, diversity, and inclusion.
With your continued support, we can ensure that racialized communities, especially those
experiencing barriers to access and opportunities, are a resource to lead, heal, thrive, and truly
belong in the City of Kitchener.
RISE is not just a vision, it is a commitment to action, equity, and transformation.
